highlights.text: whatever lies low and faces the sky
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's principal origin of the root

highlights.text: From the same origin comes al-arḍ, the earth we stand on
it never occurs in the plural in the Qurʾān
highlights.note: the entry's own note on Qur'anic usage

highlights.text: arḍ arīḍa = soft, good, fertile land (shāhid: Imruʾ al-Qays)
To put or place.
To make or fashion (ṣanaʿa).
To transform X into Y (ṣayyara)
highlights.note: e.g. making the earth a bed

highlights.text: Abū Zubayd, of a lion that has "made itself a refuge among the soft papyrus in the thicket."
jaʿala means "We made it plain (bayyannāhu)"
the root sense of ḥasad is qashr — stripping or peeling off bark
To wish that another's blessing and excellence be transferred to oneself
Shamir b. al-Ḥārith al-Ḍabbī describing jinn who come to his fire; their spokesman says: "We envy mankind the food"
citing the reply attributed to the Prophet when asked whether ghibṭ does harm
highlights.note: a sense drawn from a hadith

highlights.text: الضَّعْف (al-ḍaʿf) is the opposite of strength
ḍiʿf, "the double / multiple."
hence al-mustaḍʿafīn = those deemed weak or held down
This word is set as the opposite of istikbār ("arrogant self-magnification") in Q 34:33
The verbs aḍʿafa, ḍaʿʿafa, ḍāʿafa all = "to add to a thing its like or more."
A cited verse of poetry (unattributed) uses ḍiʿf al-widd, "double the affection."
al-Rāghib argues each of the three ḍaʿf/quwwa refers to a distinct life-stage
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 30:54

highlights.text: On the same principle Ibn ʿAbbās read Q 94:5–6
